For isotropic phase testing (Fig. 2 a-d), the simulated sphere had a refractive index of n=1.5. The illumination was simulated as monochromatic light at 550 nm with a bias retardance of π / 2 \pi/2 rad. In this simulation, we compared our phase retrieval method against Hilbert-based integration [ 1 ] , and a cumulative-sum integration with line-artifact removal (LAR) [ 32 ] ; all applied to the same simulated DIC data with diagonal ( − 45 ∘ -45^{\circ} ) shear. Because LAR was originally formulated for shear along an image axis [ 32 ] , we additionally implemented a version adapted to diagonal shear: the QPGI image is rotated by 45 ∘ 45^{\circ} so that the shear lies along x x , reconstructed with the x x -shear LAR solver, and the resulting phase is rotated back.

The regularization parameters ( λ T ​ V \lambda_{TV} for DCT+TV; μ \mu and ξ \xi for LAR, with its two spectral cut-offs at their default values) were swept over reasonable ranges and the best combination was used. At a representative noise level of 1.07% (Fig. 2 a-d, Fig. 3 b&d, Table 1 ), the Hilbert reconstruction showed the characteristic overestimation and directional streak artifacts perpendicular to the shear direction, and LAR as published left residual diagonal streaks, consistent with the known limitations of line-by-line integration for non-axis-aligned shear. Our new phase retrieval recovered a smooth phase map with the correct spatial profile, with a mild amplitude underestimation caused by the TV regularization. In this simulation the adapted LAR reached the lowest error (RMSE 0.091; SSIM 0.982), however, at the cost of four tunable parameters. Moreover, LAR requires a reliable background mask that directly enters the reconstruction itself as a constraint. In simulation, this mask is available and perfect. However, in live-cell imaging a perfect background mask is difficult to obtain, especially for images of multiple cells or moving cells. Although segmentation models such as SAM [ 12 ] (see Supplementary Material) can provide reasonably accurate masks, phase solvers that require perfect masks to push the background phase to zero essentially turn phase retrieval into a problem of cell segmentation. Instead, our new DCT+TV solver is agnostic of background and foreground and has only a single tunable parameter. Here, background pixels are only used to estimate the bias retardance and the noise level to compute SNR or CNR. To test how much each method depends on its background mask for a real live cell measurement, we reconstructed a single frame of a live cardiomyocyte recording with and without the background constraint. Fig.

2 e-h then shows the reconstructions with known background in the top-left half and the reconstruction of the same image without known background on the bottom-right half. Because LAR forces its solution to zero on every background pixel it is given, the adapted LAR reached a CNR of 31.2 on the known half, but drops 35-fold to only 0.9 on the held-out half. Instead, our new phase retrieval (5.5 and 3.5) gave similar values on both halves, since neither uses the mask in its solver. Hilbert integration (0.3 and 0.3) and LAR as published [ 32 ] did not recover the cell accurately at this diagonal shear. The high CNR of LAR on known background is therefore inflated by forcing the phase to zero outside the mask rather than relying on the measurement. Moreover, this makes the LAR method much more susceptible to uncertainty in the segmentation mask as well as to measurement noise. In a simulated noise series between 0-15% added noise (supplementary Fig. S2), the SSIM of LAR and adapted LAR drop significantly with increasing noise, while our approach stays unaffected and even outperforms LAR with perfectly known background mask for noise levels >12%. Therefore, a sphere of anisotropic retardance and angular orientation of its fast axis was simulated with 0.005 rad of retardance per pixel of thickness. At 0.115 µm/px and 550 nm that is Δ ​ n ≈ 3.8 ​ × ​ 10 − 3 \Delta n\approx 3.8×10^{-3} (Fig. 3 a-d). The analytical Stokes-based reconstruction recovered retardance with a SSIM of 0.39 at 1.07% noise level. Since this Stokes-based reconstruction is an exact analytical solution, the solutions for retardance and orientation at zero-noise are perfect (supplementary Fig. S2b, SSIM = 1.0). However, the noise sweep reveals that both retardance and orientation SSIM dropped sharply at the onset of noise ( ∼ \sim 2%) and remained approximately constant at higher noise levels ( > > 5%), indicating that the reconstruction quality is limited by the inherent sensitivity of the Stokes parameter inversion rather than by the absolute noise magnitude. Because the retardance is recovered through an inverse cosine, zero-mean intensity noise is mapped onto strictly non-negative retardance values, so the background, whose true retardance is zero, acquires a small positive noise floor (Fig. 3 c,e,i).

This floor barely affects the RMSE, but SSIM normalizes the comparison by the local signal variance and is therefore dominated by the large, structure-free background, where any deviation counts fully. The retardance reconstruction was notably more robust than orientation across all noise levels, consistent with the fact that retardance depends on the magnitude of the Stokes vector components whereas orientation depends on their ratio (see Table 1 and Supplementary Information). Next, we tested the polarimetric imaging mode of QP²I in a range of samples with different optical characteristics, including corn starch grains, highly birefringent LCE beads and fixed muscle fibers (see supplementary Methods). Fig. 3 e&f show the polarimetric reconstruction of two corn starch grains immersed in oil. The retardance map revealed the characteristic thickness-dependent birefringence profile of starch granules, with peak retardance values of approximately 0.16 rad. Assuming close to rotational symmetry for grains in a range of 6 − 13 ​ μ ​ m 6-13\penalty\ \mu m diameter, the effective birefringence would be within Δ ​ n ≈ 1 − 2.1 × 10 − 3 \Delta n\approx 1-2.1\times 10^{-3} , which is consistent with previously reported values for corn starch [ 15 ] . Additionally, the orientation map (Fig. 3 f) resolved the well-known radial fast-axis pattern of starch granules, with the reconstructed angles varying smoothly across each grain and the two grains exhibiting mutually consistent orientation fields despite differing spatial positions and orientations. To validate our retardance unwrapping framework on strongly birefringent specimens, we imaged custom LCE microspheres as shown in Fig. 3 g&h. The reconstructed retardance map (Fig. 3 g) demonstrate successful recovery of retardances far exceeding the principal [ 0 , π ] ​ rad [0,\pi]\penalty\ \text{rad} interval, reaching unwrapped values above 10 ​ rad 10\penalty\ \text{rad} . Crucially, the fast-axis orientation map (Fig.

3 h) reveal a uniform orientation field within the particle interior ( ∼ − 36 ∘ \sim-36^{\circ} ) that is completely free of the 90 ∘ 90^{\circ} jump artifacts typically induced at half-wave wrap boundaries. This confirms that wave-order determination successfully restores both quantitative retardance magnitudes and physically continuous fast-axis orientations. To demonstrate the applicability to biological tissue, crossed skeletal muscle fibers from rats were imaged in polarimetric mode (Fig. 3 i–l). The retardance map clearly resolved the two fiber bundles with distinct retardance values, and the orientation map unambiguously separated their crossing directions, appearing as opposing signs in Supplementary Fig. S3 and their orientation angles are shifted by 90 ∘ in Fig. 3 j. A line profile extracted along a single fiber (red ROI of Fig. 3 i&j) revealed periodic retardance oscillations with an amplitude of approximately 0.02 rad superimposed on a baseline of ∼ \sim 0.18 rad, corresponding to the alternating birefringent A-bands and less birefringent I-bands of the sarcomere structure. The measured retardance of 0.15–0.20 rad is consistent with the expected order of magnitude for muscle tissue (assuming a birefringence of Δ ​ n ≈ 1.79 × 10 − 3 \Delta n\approx 1.79\times 10^{-3} [ 16 ] ). The corresponding FFT of the retardance line profile (supplementary Fig. S1) yielded a single, well-defined peak indicative of a sarcomere length of 2.73 μ ​ m \mu m . 3.3 Live cell imaging of contracting CDMs We further applied QP²I to living, dynamically moving biological samples. Both QPI and polarimetric imaging modes were applied to the same cells by inserting or removing the Nomarski prisms between acquisitions. Fig. 4 shows our phase reconstruction and an AFM topography map of the same cell. Line profiles across the cell (Fig. 4 e) show a high level of agreement between the cell thickness measured by AFM and the phase profile.

Taking the AFM height of the same cell as its thickness d, the phase above the background along the profile in Fig. 4 e (0.60 – 0.77 rad over d = 3.2 – 4.6 µm) corresponds to an average refractive index of n c ​ e ​ l ​ l = n m ​ e ​ d ​ i ​ u ​ m + Δ ​ ϕ ​ λ / ( 2 ​ π ​ d ) n_{cell}=n_{medium}+\Delta\phi\lambda/(2\pi d) of 1.347 – 1.350 (assuming n m ​ e ​ d ​ i ​ u ​ m = 1.334 , λ = 550 ​ n ​ m n_{medium}=1.334,\lambda=550nm ). This is perfectly within the range of live cardiomyocytes as reported previously by intracellular microlasers [ 23 ] . While AFM provides absolute height information at nanometer axial resolution, it is fundamentally limited in temporal throughput (scan rate of 16 pixels per second, resulting in a frame rate of 0.0038 fps, see supplementary material), and requires physical contact with the sample, rendering it incompatible with live-cell dynamics. Our single-shot QPI, by contrast, operates at 87.7 megapixels/s or 70 fps (1,224 × \times 1,024 pixels per reconstruction, 2,448 × \times 2,048 pixels per raw acquisition), enabling continuous monitoring of cellular morphology changes. Fig. 4 f demonstrates this capability by showing the time-resolved phase dynamics of a spontaneously contracting cardiomyocyte, where sub-second events are captured without shear-induced spatial or motion-induced temporal artifacts. Notably, our phase reconstruction remains artifact-free even during contraction (see supplementary video), where steep local phase gradients from rapid cell deformation might produce streak artifacts in conventional Hilbert or LAR-based methods. The 20s QPI trace in Fig. 4 f shows 11 full contractions, corresponding to a contraction frequency of 0.55 Hz. During the contraction cycle, the mean phase in the ROI of Fig. 4 f changes by ∼ \sim 5%.

Under the simplifying assumption of constant thickness, which does not strictly hold because the cell compresses and relaxes, this would correspond to a refractive index modulation between 1.3487 and 1.3495, which is again of the same order as the oscillation between 1.348 - 1.354 that has been reported during CDM contractions by intracellular microlaser and were attributed to changes in sarcomeric protein density [ 23 ] . However, while QPI captures the overall cell morphology and the temporal dynamics of thickness and refractive index with high sensitivity, it fundamentally cannot visualize the contractile machinery that causes these contractions. The isotropic phase maps of live cardiomyocytes are dominated by the cell nucleus, whose elevated refractive index and substantial thickness produce a pronounced phase peak that overshadows the surrounding cytoplasm (Fig. 4 ). The contractile apparatus of the sarcomeric myofibril network, which is responsible for the mechanical contraction, contributes comparatively little to the isotropic phase signal, as the refractive index contrast between myofibrils and the surrounding cytoplasm is minimal. On the other hand, the birefringence of the aligned myosin and actin filaments within sarcomeres produces a measurable anisotropic retardance signal. The secondary polarimetric imaging contrast provides direct access to the structural organization and orientation of the contractile apparatus. Live iPSC-derived CDMs were imaged followed by fluorescence imaging of labeled sarcomeres (Fig. 5 ). Both revealed the myofibrillar network beneath and around the nucleus that could not be observed in conventional phase contrast. The retardance map resolved individual myofibrils, corresponding to an effective birefringence sensitivity of Δ ​ n eff ≈ 2.2 − 4.4 × 10 − 4 \Delta n_{\text{eff}}\approx 2.2-4.4\times 10^{-4} for an estimated myofibril thickness of ∼ \sim 1–2 μ \mu m. It was also possible to image a CDM with two adjacent myofibrils that were oriented nearly perpendicularly (supplementary Fig. S6), and the measured signed retardance showed a sign flip between both myofibrils orientated at 90 ∘ difference. This quantitative angular discrimination is analogous to the crossed-fiber result obtained for bulk muscle tissue (Fig. 3 i-l), but here achieved on the single cell level where total retardance is significantly lower.

The co-registered fluorescence confirms the spatial correspondence of the birefringent structures with the labeled sarcomeric proteins, validating that the polarimetric contrast originates from the organized contractile apparatus rather than other cellular components. Zooming onto an isolated myofibril (Fig. 5 e&f, supplementary Fig. S5e&f and S6e&f) in our retardance reconstruction revealed the repeating pattern of sarcomeres, comparable to that shown by fluorescence reference. The retardance line profile exhibits periodic oscillations corresponding to the alternating birefringent A-bands (myosin-rich) and less birefringent I-bands (actin-dominated), with notably higher modulation contrast between these bands than observed in the fluorescence channel. Furthermore, the retardance profile resolves fine sub-sarcomeric features at better contrast than in the fluorescence images of the same myofibril. For any myofibril we tested, an FFT-based analysis yielded a sarcomere length (SL) of our label-free retardance measurement that agrees with the fluorescence derrived SL within the optical resolution limit of our system (see supplementary information), confirming that the polarimetric reconstruction preserves the spatial periodicity of the sarcomeric lattice with sufficient quantitative accuracy for contractility analysis. The FFT analysis shows higher harmonics at 2 × \times , 4 × \times (Fig. 5 i). However, the bandpass filter (gray band) for determining the sarcomere length successfully rejected these. 3.4 Video-rate birefringence imaging of beating cardiomyocytes Figure 6: Time-resolved sarcomere dynamics of live cardiomyocytes. A central motivation for label-free contractility imaging is the ability to sustain high-speed recordings without the temporal and phototoxic constraints imposed by long-term fluorescence microscopy. Next, we therefore compared the ability of polarimetric imaging and conventional fluorescence imaging for the tracking of sarcomere length over time. We first recorded polarimetric retardance data at an effective frame rate of 33 fps, i.e., averaging pairs of subsequent frames to reduce reconstruction noise. The resulting evolution of retardance and sarcomere length calculated from it clearly show individual contraction–relaxation cycles (Fig. 6 a). Subsequently, a fluorescence reference was acquired from the same cardiomyocyte at 10 fps acquisition rate (i.e., 3 × \times slower sampling than the retardance imaging). Fig. 6 b shows the resulting evolution of fluorescence intensity and of the sarcomere length calculated from it, with the first contraction co-registered to the first contraction obtained from retardance-imaging. Both modalities captured 8 full contractions over the 13-second-long time-traces, corresponding to a contraction frequency of 0.66 Hz, which is comparable to the 0.55 Hz frequency observed earlier from the QPI video of a different cell (Fig. 4 f). In both modalities, signal intensity increases when sarcomere length decreases, and vice versa. This consistent trend further corroborates that both methods capture the same underlying contractile dynamics. A zoomed in comparison of two consecutive contraction events (Fig. 6 c,d) shows that the faster acquisition speed of the retardance imaging resolves additional contraction features that are not visible in the fluorescence trace.

Specifically, the retardance trace resolves fine temporal dynamics, within a single contraction event, with the contraction waveform exhibiting an intermediate relaxation and secondary peak before the final relaxation phase. These features are smoothed into a featureless plateau in the fluorescence channel (Fig. 6 d), which at 10 fps has a Nyquist-limited temporal resolution of ∼ \sim 200 ms or ∼ \sim 5 Hz. A particularly striking feature in the retardance trace is a triple-peak event that spans approximately 2.5 s and comprises a sharp retardance increase, a brief dip, an intermediate peak, a second dip, a recovery, and a sharp decrease. The sarcomere length mirrors this sequence but with an unexpected deviation: while the initial increase and final decrease show the expected anti-correlation with sarcomere length (high retardance corresponding to short sarcomeres), the intermediate peak shows a positive correlation, that is, both retardance and sarcomere length increase. This might suggest that the birefringence of the myofibril itself increases during this phase, potentially reflecting a mechanically induced change in molecular alignment (photoelasticity). A detailed biophysical interpretation of these sub-contraction dynamics is beyond the scope of the present work, but the observation demonstrates the potential of high-speed polarimetric imaging to access functional birefringence changes. Such an analysis would be inaccessible to fluorescence imaging. While in principle fluorescence acquisition rates can be increased, this comes at the cost of higher excitation intensity to maintain a sufficient signal-to-noise ratio. This in turn creates an inherent and unavoidable tradeoff: faster fluorescence imaging accelerates both photobleaching and the risk for phototoxic damage to living cell. In fact, even during our experiments, the fluorescence intensity already decayed by over 20% within only 15 seconds continuous acquisition (Fig.

6 b), and even by 70 % over a 60 s long acquisition (see supplementary Fig. S7). In contrast, the retardance signal remained constant throughout the entire recording, as the label-free birefringence contrast is inherently unaffected by photobleaching and can be read out at lower light levels, thereby also avoiding phototoxicity. This opens the possibility of arbitrarily long recording sessions, without signal degradation, enabling longitudinal studies of cardiomyocyte maturation, drug response kinetics, and fatigue that are inaccessible to fluorescence-based approaches. 4 Discussion and Conclusion In this work, we presented QP²I, as a dual-mode quantitative phase and polarimetric imaging framework that unites computational reconstruction, polarization optics, and live-cell biology. QP²I is built on a standard DIC microscope, integrating a QWP and a polarization camera. By combining a new total-variation-regularized phase solver with an analytical Stokes-based polarimetric reconstruction, we demonstrated single-shot, video-rate imaging of both isotropic and anisotropic optical properties. The new phase reconstruction addresses the susceptibility of line-integration methods to directional streak artifacts and/or the dependence on reliable segmentation masks. By formulating phase recovery as a single-stage variational problem with a shear-matched finite-difference operator, the method avoids the two-stage integrate-then-correct paradigm of previous approaches [ 1 , 32 ] and requires only a single regularization parameter. It can be implemented directly for linear as well as for diagonal shear configurations that are common in commercial DIC microscopes.

The polarimetric imaging mode extends the same hardware to quantitative birefringence measurements by removing the Nomarski prisms and using a detection QWP to encode the circular polarization component of the sample, which carries the retardance information, into the linearly polarized channels measurable by a conventional polarization camera. This analytical Stokes inversion, computed in a single pass without iterative optimization, recovered both retardance and fast-axis orientation maps at the full camera frame rate. The synergy of these two modalities proved particularly powerful for label-free imaging of live cardiomyocyte, where QPI and polarimetry provide complementary information of the same cell. The isotropic phase maps captured overall cell morphology based on height and refractive index differences, which is dominated by the nucleus and was validated against co-registered AFM topography data. The polarimetric maps of the same cells selectively revealed the birefringent contractile myofibrillar architecture that is invisible to conventional phase contrast. Together, these modalities enabled simultaneous monitoring of cellular morphology and sarcomere organization during spontaneous contraction at an effective frame rate of up to 70 fps at full megapixel resolution. Crucially, this frame rate was not limited by biological constraints from the sample, optical constraints of the microscope, or computational constraints of the reconstruction algorithm, but was determined solely by the camera electronics. The temporal resolution was sufficient to capture fast contraction dynamics, including double-pump waveforms and complex sub-contraction events that were not resolved in the co-registered fluorescence reference at 10 fps. Moreover, the intrinsic birefringence contrast remained constant throughout extended recordings, while the fluorescence signal decayed by over 70% within 60 s.

These results establish QP²I as a physiologically gentle alternative for sustained contractility analysis. The sensitivity of QP²I to these detailed dynamics might help answer a long-standing open question about functional muscle biophysics, namely, whether active contraction increases or decreases the optical retardance of the myofibril. Classical bulk measurements have reported both transient increases [ 2 ] and decreases [ 6 ] in birefringence during activation, reflecting competing contributions from myosin head reorientation, filament overlap changes, and fiber geometry [ 11 , 9 ] . Critically, these studies were confined to bulk preparations or skinned fibers. Our results now suggest that sarcomere length and retardance signal are anti-correlated, however, that sub-contraction events can show transient departures from this anti-correlation (Fig. 6 ). High-speed single-cell polarimetry might therefore allow to revisit the question about contraction induced changes in intrinsic retardance at the individual cardiomyocyte level, disentangling geometric and molecular contributions through simultaneous retardance, orientation, and sarcomere length tracking within single contraction cycles. Some limitations of the current implementation merit discussion. The four linear micropolarizers of the camera cannot distinguish left- from right-handed circular polarization, introducing a sign ambiguity in the Stokes component and consequently in the reconstructed orientation of the fast axis θ \theta . In order to maintain quantitative retardance with the same net η \eta value for structures at any in-plane orientation (e.g., the same quantitative η \eta for all myofibrils at different angles), the polarimetric reconstruction was deliberately designed for η \eta without orientation bias, at the cost of reduced θ \theta determination.

However, by rotating the second QWP by 45 ∘ , the same pipeline could also be used to reconstruct θ \theta more cleanly at the cost of greater ambiguity in η \eta . In future works, for samples with low birefringence, this trade-off as well as the sign ambiguity could be completely resolved by using a second synchronized polarization camera with an additional QWP at 45 ∘ orientation to directly measure all 4 Stokes parameters (see supplementary material for more detail). In the QPI mode, the phase gradient image is extracted via atan2 \operatorname{atan2} , which wraps at ± π \pm\pi and therefore limits the maximum measurable phase gradient per shear distance. This constraint is relevant for thick, high-contrast samples such as glass microspheres but less so for thin biological specimens. Strongly birefringent samples present an additional subtlety in DIC-to-QPI methods: in DIC microscopy, two orthogonally polarized, laterally sheared beams accumulate different optical path lengths and interfere to produce phase-gradient contrast. However, in birefringent samples, these orthogonally polarized beams also experience different refractive indices at the same spatial position, producing a differential phase delay that is indistinguishable from the isotropic phase gradient. This ambiguity is inherent to any DIC-to-QPI method, and was apparent in our QP²I of single cardiomyocytes, where faint myofibrillar signatures emerged in the phase maps. Importantly, this cross-talk affects only the isotropic phase reconstruction, while the polarimetric imaging mode, without Nomarski prisms, remains unaffected. The availability of both modalities on the same instrument thus provides an intrinsic consistency check: structures appearing in both phase and retardance maps can be identified as birefringent, enabling disambiguation that would not be possible with either modality alone.

Another potential limitation is the decrease in effective resolution caused by using a sub-grid of 2 × \times 2 polarizer pixels as virtual super-pixel for the reconstruction. Since most experiments throughout this work were carried out with a 100 × \times magnification, the effective pixel size of the reconstructions was 69 nm which is still well below the optical resolution limit. However, the use of lower magnification objectives might be affected. The system operates at 87.7 megapixels per second and is limited only by the camera readout electronics. Polarization-sensitive sensors with higher pixel counts (up to 4096 × \times 3000) already exist commercially, and advances in sensor electronics that increase overall pixel throughput per time would directly translate to higher frame rates or larger fields of view of QP²I without any modification to the optical setup or reconstruction software. A natural extension of the current work is volumetric imaging through axial scanning, which would directly enable three-dimensional QPI and polarimetric tomography at rates potentially exceeding those of competing sequential-illumination volume scanning approaches such as tensorial Fourier ptychography [ 30 , 33 ] , which require hundreds of LED acquisitions per volume. Three-dimensional high-speed polarimetry would be of particular interest for thick muscle tissue. Such volumetric birefringence data could leverage existing three-dimensional muscle morphology analysis tools originally developed for second-harmonic generation (SHG) microscopy [ 21 , 26 ] , which is a significantly more expensive and complex nonlinear imaging modality compared to QP²I.

Beyond muscle cells and tissue, QP²I could open applications of label-free imaging of intrinsic phase and birefringence contrast at video rate, including cancer research (e.g., extracellular matrix organization in tumor microenvironments), neuroscience (e.g., myelination dynamics), and fibrosis (e.g., fibrotic tissue remodeling), where our sustained, non-perturbative observation of molecular-scale organization at video rate could complement or replace current fluorescence-based assays.
